name: Downward-Facing Dog
description: Downward-facing dog is a foundational yoga posture that simultaneously stretches the hamstrings, calves, and latissimus dorsi while building shoulder stability and core engagement. With the hips raised into an inverted V shape and heels pressed toward the floor, the entire posterior chain is loaded in a lengthened position. It is used extensively as a transitional movement in yoga, as a warm-up for athletic activities, and as a standalone mobility exercise.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a push-up or tabletop position with hands shoulder-width apart and feet hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat to prevent hand and foot slipping.
steps: Step 1: Begin from a tabletop on hands and knees or a push-up position.
Step 2: Press through the palms and lift the hips toward the ceiling, straightening the knees and forming an inverted V.
Step 3: Press the heels toward the floor. They need not touch — a stretch in the calves and hamstrings should be felt.
Step 4: Externally rotate the arms slightly so the elbow creases face forward.
Step 5: Hold 30–60 seconds, pressing firmly through the hands and reaching the hips high.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe slowly and deeply. Exhale and press the hips higher. Inhale and settle into the position.
common_mistakes: Rounding the upper back and collapsing the shoulder blades — press through the hands and spread them
Not pressing the heels toward the floor — work toward this even if the calves are tight
Bending the knees excessively, which reduces the hamstring and calf stretch
safety_considerations: Wrist discomfort is common — reduce by turning fingertips outward or using fists or push-up handles
Shoulder injuries: consult a clinician before including overhead loaded positions
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The goal is a straight spine from hands to hips and heels as close to the floor as the posterior chain allows.
coaching_cues: Press the floor away with your hands
Reach the tailbone toward the ceiling
Press your heels toward the floor — imagine footprints on a mat
